canonicalExplanation.summary: Ignoring a promise doesn't stop the work behind it; the request keeps running and its result can still arrive. To cancel, create an **AbortController**, pass `controller.signal` to fetch, and call `controller.abort()` when the result is no longer wanted. The fetch then rejects with an error named **"AbortError"**, which is intentional and should be ignored quietly, while real network failures still get reported. `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` gives you a timeout the same way; its error is named **"TimeoutError"**.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner types "arr" then "array" into a lesson search. The "arr" request is slow and finishes last, so the list shows results for "arr" under the word "array". A new search aborts the previous fetch and ignores its AbortError while reporting real network failures. In this lesson you'll implement and test cancellation or latest-request-wins behavior for an interactive fetch.

```predict
{"question": "`let p = fetch(\"/api/search?q=arr\"); p = null;` Is the request cancelled?", "options": ["Yes, nothing references it", "No: the request keeps going; only abort() cancels it"], "answer": 1, "why": "Dropping the variable only means you can't see the result. The network request still completes."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know the **Call stack and event loop model**, **Closures and lifetime** (the controller lives in a closure), **Fetch and HTTP responses**, and **Event propagation and delegation**, because typing fires input events.

sections.heading: The model: one controller per request, abort the old one
Latest request wins

includes: Cancel fetches with AbortController and signal.
Tell AbortError and TimeoutError apart from real failures; implement latest-request-wins.
excludes: Cancelling non-fetch APIs you write yourself in depth.

outcomes: Implement and test cancellation or latest-request-wins behavior for an interactive fetch.

examples.title: The search box that showed old results
examples.situation: A new search aborts the previous fetch and ignores its AbortError while reporting real network failures.
walkthrough: **Aborts the previous fetch:** typing "array" calls `controller.abort()` on the "arr" request before starting a new one.
**Ignores its AbortError:** the old request rejects with AbortError, and the catch returns quietly.
**Test:** a fake slow fetch for "arr" and fast one for "array" will leave only "array" results rendered, and a TypeError will show the error message.
examples.result: The list always matches the latest search text, and genuine failures are still reported.

examples.title: The spinner that never stopped
examples.situation: A report download sometimes hangs for minutes on a bad connection, and the spinner never goes away.
walkthrough: fetch has no default timeout, so it can wait a very long time.
Pass `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10000)` to give up after 10 seconds.
In catch, check `error.name === "TimeoutError"` and show "This is taking too long. Try again.".
examples.result: After 10 seconds the spinner stops and the learner sees a clear timeout message.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Dropping a promise variable automatically cancels its underlying request.
misconceptions.correction: A promise is only a result placeholder. The request behind it keeps running until it finishes or an AbortSignal cancels it. Use AbortController to stop it.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, why did the request keep going?

analogy.example: An AbortController is like **the cancel button on a taxi app**. Closing the app (dropping the promise) doesn't stop the taxi coming. Pressing cancel (abort) tells the driver to stop, and the "ride cancelled" notice (AbortError) isn't a problem to report.
limitations: Taxis charge fees; aborts are free.
A timeout is like auto-cancelling if the taxi isn't there in 10 minutes.

artifact: A rejects with AbortError; B renders

steps.explanation: The first request starts with its own abort signal.
A new search aborts the previous fetch before starting another.
It ignores the AbortError while real network failures are still reported.

nearTransfer.prompt: Add a 5-second timeout to `getLesson(id)` with AbortSignal.timeout, and show "Taking too long" for TimeoutError while other errors keep their messages.

farTransfer.prompt: Build a type-ahead search with abort, a timeout via AbortSignal.any, and tests using fake fetches that resolve out of order. Prove only the latest results render and timeouts show a message.
expectedEvidence: Timeout and network errors show distinct messages.

remediation.explanation: For every request that a newer action can replace, ask: **who owns its AbortController, and when do I call abort()?** In every catch, check error.name before reporting.
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The spinner that never stopped".

recap.summary: To implement and test cancellation or latest-request-wins behavior, give each fetch an AbortController signal, abort the previous request when a new one starts, ignore AbortError, give timeouts their own TimeoutError message, and still report real network and HTTP failures.
